title: The Email Intelligence Suite — Build 3 Email Skills

sections.content:
## What You'll Build

By the end of this lesson you'll have three permanently saved email skills:

1. **`/email-sort`** — reads your inbox and sorts it into action categories automatically
2. **`/email-report`** — weekly email analytics: volume, top senders, what needs response
3. **`/email-draft $ARGUMENTS`** — context-aware reply drafter that reads the thread first

These aren't demos. After this lesson, you'll run `/email-sort` on Monday mornings and `/email-report` on Fridays as part of your actual workflow. The skills stay on your machine, work with your real inbox, and save you 30–45 minutes per week.
**Prerequisite:** Gmail MCP must be connected. Check with `/mcp` in Claude Code — `gmail` or `claude_ai_Gmail` should appear as connected. If not, complete lesson 8-11 first to set up the Gmail MCP.

## Skill 1: /email-sort — Intelligent Inbox Sorting

The `/email-sort` skill reads your inbox, categorises every unread email, applies Gmail labels, and produces a triage report. The first time you run it it will feel like magic — but it's just a well-designed skill using the Gmail MCP tools.

**What it does:**
- Counts unread emails
- Searches for emails needing action (direct questions, requests, deadlines)
- Identifies emails you're waiting on (threads where you sent last)
- Finds newsletters and bulk mail to archive
- Applies Gmail labels: `TODO`, `Waiting`, `Newsletter`, `FYI`
- Produces a short triage report

**The complete skill file:**

```markdown
# /email-sort — Intelligent Inbox Triage

<role>
You are an expert email triage assistant with access to Gmail MCP tools.
You understand how to read intent from email subject lines, senders, and
body content. Your job is to sort my inbox efficiently and apply labels
so I know exactly what needs my attention.
</role>

<context>
The user's inbox may have anywhere from 5 to 500 unread emails. Prioritise
accuracy over speed — it is better to process fewer emails correctly than
to misclassify many. The user will review the triage report and can correct
misclassifications.
</context>

<steps>
1. Count total unread emails using Gmail search: `is:unread label:inbox`
2. Find ACTION emails: unread threads where I was directly asked a question,
   given a task, or where a deadline is mentioned — apply label `TODO`
3. Find WAITING emails: threads where my last message was the most recent
   and I'm expecting a reply — apply label `Waiting`
4. Find NEWSLETTER emails: unread emails with unsubscribe links from senders
   I've never replied to — apply label `Newsletter`
5. Find FYI emails: informational emails (announcements, CC'd on things,
   notifications) that need no action — apply label `FYI`
6. Leave anything ambiguous unlabelled and note it in the report
</steps>

<output>
After completing all steps, produce this report:

**📥 Inbox Triage Complete**

Total unread: [X]

| Category | Count | Top items |
|----------|-------|----------|
| ✅ TODO | [n] | [top 2 senders/subjects] |
| ⏳ Waiting | [n] | [top 2 threads] |
| 📰 Newsletter | [n] | [top 2 senders] |
| ℹ️ FYI | [n] | [brief description] |
| ❓ Unclear | [n] | [brief description] |

**Most urgent TODO:**
[The single most time-sensitive email, with sender + subject + why it's urgent]

**Recommended next action:** [1 specific thing to do right now]
</output>

<constraints>
- Process a maximum of 50 unread emails per run (most recent first)
- If more than 50 unread exist, note '[X] older emails not processed — run again after clearing these'
- Do not draft replies — just categorise
- Do not archive or delete — only apply labels
- If a label doesn't exist yet, create it before applying it
</constraints>

<fallback>
If Gmail MCP is not connected: explain that /email-sort requires Gmail MCP
and link to lesson 8-11 for setup instructions.
If no unread emails exist: report 'Inbox clear — 0 unread emails.'
</fallback>
```

Save this as `~/.claude/commands/email-sort.md`.

## Skill 2: /email-report — Weekly Email Analytics

The `/email-report` skill gives you a weekly view of your email patterns: who you're communicating with most, what topics dominate your inbox, which threads are unresolved, and where your email time is going.

Run this every Friday afternoon or Monday morning for a high-level view of your communication landscape.

**The complete skill file:**

```markdown
# /email-report — Weekly Email Analytics

<role>
You are an email analytics assistant. You read email data and produce
clear, actionable insights — not just counts, but patterns and implications.
</role>

<steps>
1. Count total emails received in the last 7 days (search: `newer_than:7d`)
2. Find the top 10 senders by volume in the last 7 days
3. Count emails where I was the only recipient vs. emails I was CC'd on
4. Find all threads started in the last 7 days where I haven't replied yet
5. Count emails I sent in the last 7 days
6. Find the longest active thread (most back-and-forth) in the last 7 days
7. Identify any recurring senders I haven't subscribed to but appear weekly
</steps>

<output>
**📊 Weekly Email Report — [Current week dates]**

**Volume**
- Received: [X] | Sent: [X] | Net: [+/- X]
- Solo recipient: [X]% | CC'd only: [X]%

**Top Senders This Week**
1. [Sender] — [X] emails — [brief topic]
2. [Sender] — [X] emails — [brief topic]
3. [Sender] — [X] emails — [brief topic]
(up to 5)

**Unresolved Threads** ([X] total)
- [Subject] from [Sender] — [X] days old — [why it's likely important]
(up to 3 most important)

**Most Active Thread:** [Subject] — [X] messages

**Patterns & Recommendations**
- [1-2 observations about communication patterns this week]
- [1 specific recommendation: e.g., 'You have 5 unresolved threads with clients — worth a reply batch today']

**Action:** [The single most valuable email task to do right now]
</output>

<constraints>
- Keep total under 300 words
- Recommendations must be specific and actionable, not generic
- Don't list every email — identify patterns
</constraints>

<fallback>
If fewer than 10 emails in the last 7 days: note this and shorten the report accordingly.
If Gmail MCP unavailable: explain the requirement and stop.
</fallback>
```

Save this as `~/.claude/commands/email-report.md`.

## Skill 3: /email-draft — Context-Aware Reply Drafter

The `/email-draft` skill is the most practically useful of the three. You pass it a sender name or subject, it reads the full thread, understands the context, and drafts a reply in your voice.

The key design decision: it reads the thread first, then asks what you want to say (if you haven't specified), then drafts — never the other way around. This prevents replies that miss context from earlier in the thread.

**The complete skill file:**

```markdown
# /email-draft — Context-Aware Reply Drafter

<role>
You are my email writing assistant. You read email threads carefully before
drafting — never guess at context. You write in a professional but natural
tone: direct, not stiff; warm, not casual. You do not use filler phrases
like 'I hope this email finds you well' or 'Please don't hesitate to reach out.'
</role>

<steps>
1. If $ARGUMENTS is provided: search Gmail for threads matching $ARGUMENTS
   (treat it as a sender name, subject keyword, or thread description)
   If no argument: find the most recent email in my inbox that needs a reply
2. Read the complete thread — every message, in order
3. Identify: What is being asked of me? What is the context? What has already been agreed?
4. If the user hasn't told me what to say: briefly summarise the situation and ask
   'What would you like your reply to say?' then wait
5. Once you know what the user wants to say: draft a complete, professional reply
6. Save the draft using Gmail MCP create_draft tool
</steps>

<output>
First, show a thread summary:
---
**Thread:** [Subject]
**From:** [Sender] | **Date:** [date of most recent message]
**Summary:** [2 sentences: what this thread is about and what's being asked of me]
---

Then, if I told you what to say, produce the draft immediately.
If I haven't told you: ask what I'd like to say.

Draft format:
---
**DRAFT REPLY:**

Hi [Name],

[Body of reply]

[Sign-off],
[My name]
---

After the draft: 'This has been saved as a Gmail draft. Review and send from Gmail.'
</output>

<constraints>
- Never send — only create a draft
- Do not invent facts about the thread that aren't in the emails
- Keep replies under 200 words unless the thread requires more
- Do not apologise unnecessarily or use corporate filler phrases
- Match the formality of the incoming email
</constraints>

<fallback>
If no matching thread found: 'No thread found matching "$ARGUMENTS". Try a different
search term (sender name, subject word, or date range).'
</fallback>
```

Save this as `~/.claude/commands/email-draft.md`.

sections.title: Build & Test All Three Email Skills
sections.content:
Create all three email skills and run each one on your real inbox.

**Step 1 — Create the skills directory (if not already done):**
```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path ~/.claude/commands
```

**Step 2 — Create email-sort.md:**
In Claude Code:
```
Create ~/.claude/commands/email-sort.md with the /email-sort skill content
from lesson 20-3.
```
(Paste the skill content from the lesson, or ask Claude to write it from the description.)

**Step 3 — Create email-report.md:**
```
Create ~/.claude/commands/email-report.md with the /email-report skill content.
```

**Step 4 — Create email-draft.md:**
```
Create ~/.claude/commands/email-draft.md with the /email-draft skill content.
```

**Step 5 — Verify all three exist:**
```
List all files in ~/.claude/commands/
```
You should see: `daily-brief.md`, `email-sort.md`, `email-report.md`, `email-draft.md` (and any others from previous lessons).

**Step 6 — Run /email-sort:**
```
/email-sort
```
Watch it read your inbox and apply labels. Check Gmail — the labels should appear.

**Step 7 — Run /email-report:**
```
/email-report
```
Read the analytics. Does it match your sense of your inbox this week?

**Step 8 — Run /email-draft on a real email:**
```
/email-draft [name of someone who emailed you this week]
```
Review the draft. How close is it to what you'd actually send?

**Step 9 — Improve one skill based on what you saw:**
After running all three, identify the biggest improvement opportunity in any one skill. Ask Claude:
```
Update ~/.claude/commands/[skill-name].md to [specific improvement].
```

**Accomplishment check:** All three skills created, all three run on real data, at least one improved based on real results.

sections.title: Workshop A — Build an /email-unsubscribe Skill
sections.content:
Build a fourth email skill that finds newsletters and subscription emails you no longer read, extracts their unsubscribe links, and presents them for one-click unsubscribing.

**Why this matters:** Unsubscribing manually requires opening each email, finding the small link at the bottom, clicking through, waiting for confirmation. For 10 subscriptions, that's 20 minutes. This skill does the search in 30 seconds and gives you the links all at once.

**Step 1 — Design the skill:**
Before writing any code, answer:
- What Gmail search query finds newsletter/subscription emails?
- How do you identify emails with unsubscribe links vs regular emails?
- What's the best way to present 10+ unsubscribe links without overwhelming?
- What should the skill do if an unsubscribe link can't be found in the email body?

**Step 2 — Write the skill:**
```
Write ~/.claude/commands/email-unsubscribe.md:

This skill should:
1. Search for emails with unsubscribe links from senders I've received 3+ emails from
2. For each sender: count how many emails I've received from them in the last 90 days
3. Check if I've ever REPLIED to any of their emails
4. If I've never replied: include them in the 'consider unsubscribing' list
5. Extract the unsubscribe link from their most recent email
6. Present a ranked list: highest volume senders first, with their unsubscribe link

Output format: a clean list I can scan quickly, with each sender on one line.
Do NOT automatically unsubscribe — just show me the links.
```

**Step 3 — Test it:**
```
/email-unsubscribe
```
How many subscriptions does it find? Are any surprising?

**Step 4 — Act on the results:**
For each subscription you want to stop:
- Click the unsubscribe link
- Confirm the unsubscription
- Note how long it takes vs manually finding each link

**Outcome:** An unsubscribe skill that finds inbox clutter in 30 seconds and presents all the links you need to clean it up.

sections.title: Workshop B — Personalise /email-draft to Your Voice
sections.content:
The generic /email-draft skill writes in a professional but neutral tone. This workshop teaches you to personalise it to match your actual writing style.

**Step 1 — Capture your voice:**
```
Read the last 10 emails I sent (use Gmail MCP: search `from:me newer_than:30d`
and read the sent emails). Based on these, describe:
- My typical email length
- My greeting style (Hi, Hello, Hey, [Name])
- My sign-off style
- My tone (formal/informal, direct/chatty)
- Phrases I use frequently
- What I avoid (do I skip 'I hope this finds you well'?)
```

**Step 2 — Update the skill with your voice profile:**
```
Update ~/.claude/commands/email-draft.md:

In the <role> section, add this voice profile based on what you found:
'Write in [Your Name]'s voice: [tone], [length], greeting '[their greeting style]',
sign-off '[their sign-off]'. Avoid: [phrases they never use].'
```

**Step 3 — Test with a real email:**
```
/email-draft [sender name]
```
Does the draft now sound more like you?

**Step 4 — Run an A/B test:**
For the same email, ask Claude:
```
Draft two versions of a reply to [sender] about [topic]:
Version A: using my voice profile in /email-draft
Version B: generic professional email
Show both side by side.
```
Which one would you actually send?

**Outcome:** An `/email-draft` skill that writes in your actual voice — not a generic corporate AI voice.

sections.question: The /email-sort skill is designed to process a maximum of 50 unread emails per run. Why is this constraint important?
options: Gmail MCP can only handle 50 API calls
Processing too many emails at once can cause Claude to run out of context window, making later classifications less accurate — the limit ensures quality across all processed emails
50 is the maximum number of Gmail labels allowed
Claude Code has a 50-message limit per session
sections.explanation: Processing many emails in a single run can degrade quality as the context window fills up — Claude may start making less accurate classifications toward the end because there's less 'room' for careful reasoning. The 50-email limit ensures consistent quality across all processed emails. For inboxes with hundreds of unread emails, it's better to run the skill multiple times, clearing each batch, than to attempt everything at once with degrading accuracy.

sections.question: The /email-draft skill reads the full thread before drafting. Why does this matter for email quality?
options: It doesn't matter — the most recent email has all the information needed

Reading the full thread prevents replies that miss earlier context, contradict previously agreed decisions, or re-ask questions already answered — it produces replies that feel natural rather than AI-generated
Reading the full thread is required by Gmail API
It makes the draft longer and more comprehensive
sections.explanation: Context from earlier messages critically shapes what a good reply says. Common AI email mistakes — 'Can you send me that document?' when the document was shared 3 messages ago, or agreeing to something already declined — all happen when the AI only sees the most recent message. Reading the full thread means the draft accounts for what's already been said, agreed, shared, or declined — producing replies that feel like they came from someone who was paying attention.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 20-3.** You've built three email skills that work on your real inbox: `/email-sort` for triage, `/email-report` for weekly analytics, and `/email-draft` for context-aware replies. These alone can save 30+ minutes per week. Next: the most powerful skill pattern in this course — using 5 parallel subagents to eliminate hallucination.
